\subsubsection{The transimpedance loop}\label{sss:tia-loop}

The loop is stable with \SIrange{61.2}{64.9}{\degree} of phase margin and
\SIrange{1.2}{1.5}{\decibel} of peaking at maximum gain
(Tables~\ref{tab:tia-cl-stability} and~\ref{tab:tia-cl-transfer}), given
\SI{22}{\pico\farad} of feedback capacitance. An earlier revision of this section
reported \SIrange{5.0}{6.4}{\decibel} of peaking and a feedback capacitor of order
\SI{200}{\pico\farad}, which would have been \SI{0.1}{\milli\metre\squared} of MIM per
channel across four channels. That figure was a property of the testbench: it loaded the
working electrode with a bare capacitance to ground rather than the cell model of
Figure~\ref{fig:randles-cell}.

\paragraph{Why the load model decides the answer.} Writing $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ for the
impedance from the summing node to AC ground, the noise gain is
$1/\beta = 1 + R_f/Z_{\mathrm{in}}$. A bare capacitor gives
$Z_{\mathrm{in}} = 1/sC_{\mathrm{dl}}$, so $1/\beta$ rises without bound at
\SI{20}{\decibel} per decade and meets the amplifier's own roll-off at a
\SI{40}{\decibel}-per-decade rate of closure --- phase margin tends to zero by
construction. A real electrode places the solution resistance $R_s$ in series with the
double layer,

\begin{equation}\label{eq:tia-beta}
  Z_{\mathrm{in}}(s) = R_s + \left( R_{\mathrm{ct}} \parallel \frac{1}{sC_{\mathrm{dl}}} \right),
  \qquad
  \frac{1}{\beta} \longrightarrow 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_s}
  \quad \text{for } f \gg \frac{1}{2\pi R_s C_{\mathrm{dl}}},
\end{equation}

so the noise gain flattens and the loop closes at \SI{20}{\decibel} per decade instead.
The zero that does this is the electrode's, not the designer's.

\paragraph{The residual requirement.} $R_s$ alone is not sufficient across the declared
electrode spread. At $R_s = \SI{1}{\kilo\ohm}$ the zero lands at \SI{1.6}{\kilo\hertz},
below crossover, and margin reaches \SIrange{89.8}{90.6}{\degree} with no feedback
capacitor at all. At $R_s = \SI{100}{\ohm}$ it lands at \SI{15.9}{\kilo\hertz}, above
crossover, and margin falls to \SIrange{35.7}{40.3}{\degree}. \SI{22}{\pico\farad}
across $R_f$ supplies the missing lead and holds every combination of
$R_s \in \{\SI{100}{\ohm},\ \SI{1}{\kilo\ohm}\}$,
$C_{\mathrm{dl}} \in \{\SI{100}{\nano\farad},\ \SI{1}{\micro\farad}\}$ and
$R_f \in \{\SI{35}{\kilo\ohm},\ \SI{560}{\kilo\ohm}\}$ above \SI{61}{\degree}, at a cost
of about \SI{0.011}{\milli\metre\squared} per channel. Peaking agrees independently:
the \SI{2}{\decibel} criterion is met at \SI{22}{\pico\farad} and missed at
\SI{5}{\pico\farad} and \SI{10}{\pico\farad}.

\SI{100}{\nano\farad} is the stressing case and \SI{10}{\micro\farad} the benign one,
which is the opposite of the assumption this bench was originally written against.
Smaller double-layer capacitance pushes crossover out towards the amplifier's second
pole; larger capacitance drops the feedback pole and pulls crossover in. The noise trade
runs the other way --- input-referred current noise over \SIrange{0.1}{100}{\hertz} is
\SI{0.48}{\nano\ampere} at \SI{100}{\nano\farad} against
\SIrange{2.2}{2.4}{\nano\ampere} at \SI{1}{\micro\farad} --- so the two cannot be
optimised together.

\paragraph{What now limits the stage is DC loop gain, not phase.} With
$R_{\mathrm{ct}} = \SI{1}{\mega\ohm}$ the loop has \SIrange{76.5}{78.0}{\decibel} and
transimpedance sits within \SI{0.02}{\percent} of $R_f$. With
$R_{\mathrm{ct}} = \SI{10}{\kilo\ohm}$ the electrode shunts the summing node,
$\beta_{\mathrm{DC}} = \SI{10.1}{\kilo\ohm} / \SI{570}{\kilo\ohm}$, and only
\SIrange{41.9}{44.3}{\decibel} remains. The consequences are a gain error of
\SIrange{-1.24}{-0.98}{\percent}, an input offset multiplied by the same noise gain to
\SIrange{-9.9}{-4.1}{\milli\volt} against a \SI{5}{\milli\volt} budget, and genuine
non-linearity of \SIrange{1.27}{1.65}{} LSB once gain and offset are fitted out. No
capacitor addresses any of this. It is the same shortage of open-loop gain into a
low-impedance cell that Section~\ref{ss:controlamp} reports for the control amplifier.
Whether \SI{10}{\kilo\ohm} is a credible charge-transfer resistance for the intended
electrode is the open question, and it decides whether this stage needs a second gain
stage.

\paragraph{Coverage.} These figures are schematic-level over five process corners at
\SI{25}{\celsius}, with an \emph{ideal} feedback resistor rather than the 16-tap
programmable string, and with no Monte Carlo --- so nothing here bounds mismatch, and
the offset quoted above is the systematic part only. The sourcing limit of
Table~\ref{tab:tia-drive} is independent of everything in this section and remains
open.
